Hexagon size is one of those topics beekeepers can debate for hours, but it fundamentally comes down to biological control and pest management. In beekeeping, cell size dictates the "caste" of the bee that will be born in that cell.

1. The Critical Dimension: $5.4\text{mm}$ vs. $4.9\text{mm}$

Most commercial foundation (the stuff you saw at Theisen's) is standardized at $5.4\text{mm}$. This is technically "large-cell" foundation.

  • Standard ($5.4\text{mm}$): Historically, beekeepers thought bigger cells would grow bigger bees, who could carry more nectar. While the bees are larger, research has shown they aren't necessarily more productive.
  • Natural/Small Cell ($4.9\text{mm}$): This is closer to what bees build in the wild. Many hobbyists prefer this because smaller cells produce smaller bees that emerge from their cocoons roughly 2 days faster than large-cell bees.

2. Why the Size Matters (The Mite Factor)

The size matters most because of Varroa Mites, the #1 threat to bees in Iowa.

  • The Race Against Time: Varroa mites reproduce inside the capped cells while the bee is developing. Because "small cell" bees emerge a couple of days earlier, the mites have less time to complete their reproductive cycle.
  • Tracheal Mites: Some studies suggest that the smaller physical size of "natural" bees makes it harder for tracheal mites to enter their breathing tubes.

3. The "Drone" Trap

If you make your hexagons too large (anything over $6.0\text{mm}$), the Queen will see them as Drone Cells (male bees).

  • The Consequence: Drones don't collect nectar; they only eat and wait to mate. A hive with too many drones can't store enough honey for the winter.
  • Your 3D Print: Since you are using a 15-20% Honeycomb Infill on your Bambu Lab A1, you are aiming for that $5.4\text{mm}$ range. If your infill looks like "large holes," you'll end up with a hive full of drones.

Using silicone caulk on your hive is a classic "good in theory, tricky in practice" scenario. While it seems like a great way to seal those puzzle-piece (box) joints, it can actually create more work for you—and the bees—down the line.

Here is the breakdown of why you might want to skip the caulk for the internal edges and where it actually is useful.

1. The "Bees Already Have Caulk" Rule

Bees produce a substance called propolis (often called "bee glue"). It’s a sticky resin they gather from trees, and they use it specifically to seal every tiny crack, gap, and draft in the hive.

  • If you seal it: You’re taking away a natural job the bees are programmed to do.
  • If they don't like your seal: They might actually spend time chewing out your silicone to replace it with their own antimicrobial propolis.

2. The Moisture Trap Problem

In Iowa, the biggest killer of bees isn't the cold—it's moisture.

  • Condensation: Bees generate a lot of heat. If you seal the hive completely "airtight" with silicone, that warm, moist air hits the ceiling, turns into water, and drips back down on the bees. A wet bee in 30-degree weather is a dead bee.
  • Breathability: You actually want those tiny microscopic gaps in the wood joints to allow a very small amount of gas exchange.

3. Where Silicone Is a Good Idea

If you still want to use it, keep it to the exterior only and the non-moving parts:

  • Outer Joints: Applying a bead of silicone to the outside of your box joints (the fingers) can prevent rainwater from wicking into the end-grain of the wood. This helps your hive last for years rather than rotting out.
  • The Bottom Board: If your bottom board has a large crack or a loose seam where it meets the landing porch, a dab of silicone there is fine to keep the wind from whistling through the floor.
  • The "Puzzle Pieces": If your box joints are a bit loose and the box feels "wobbly," use Titebond III Wood Glue (available at Theisen's of Ames) instead of silicone. It’s waterproof, food-safe, and will actually provide the structural strength silicone lacks.

Ah, the classic "disappearing paint" mystery. If you put a layer on and the wood still looks exactly the same, you didn't accidentally buy clear coat—you almost certainly ran into one of two very common woodworking/painting traps.

Since you need this hive ready to protect your bees from the Iowa sun, here is exactly what happened and how to fix it fast.

Diagnosis 1: You Used White "Stain" or "Wash" Instead of Paint

If the label says "White Pickling Stain," "Solid Color Stain," or "Chalk Wash," it is designed by default to sink into the wood pores rather than build a solid plastic layer on top.

  • The Result: It leaves a faint, translucent tint but lets the raw pine wood grain show right through. It won't give you that bright, heat-reflecting white protective shell your hive needs.

Diagnosis 2: The Wood "Drank" It (The Raw Pine Sponge Effect)

Raw, untreated pine is incredibly thirsty. If you applied a standard latex or water-based exterior paint directly to the raw wood without a primer, the dry wood fibers act like a sponge. They will instantly suck the liquid vehicle (water/oil) straight out of the paint and deep into the board, leaving a incredibly thin, faint layer of pigment on the surface that looks like it barely changed the color.

How to Fix It Right Now

Since your bees are the priority, you need a solid, reflective coat of white on the outside of the hive body to keep the colony from overheating this summer.

  1. Step 1: Use a Dedicated Primer (or a "Paint + Primer" In One) You need a high-solids exterior primer (like KILZ or Zinsser) or a thick exterior paint that explicitly states "Paint + Primer." The primer's job is to chemically seal those thirsty wood pores so your actual color coat can sit proudly on top of the wood instead of sinking into it.
  2. Step 2: Slap on a Second Coat Even with the right paint, raw wood almost always requires two coats. The first coat seals the wood; the second coat gives you that solid, protective, brilliant white finish.
  3. Step 3: Only Paint the Outside! Make sure you are only painting the exterior faces of your hive boxes. Leave the inside walls completely raw and unpainted—the bees prefer the natural wood texture and will seal the interior themselves using propolis.

If you need to grab a quick, heavy-duty quart of exterior white primer or a true "one-coat" exterior paint to get this knocked out, Theisen's or Menards right off Highway 30 will have exactly what you need to get that box bright white before the heat hits.

turns.prompt_text: What is primer
turns.response_html:
Think of primer as the insurance policy for your paint job. It isn’t actually paint—it is a specialized preparatory coating designed to act as a chemical bridge between the raw material (like your pine wood) and your final topcoat of paint.

While paint is packed with pigment to give you color, primer is packed with resins and binders designed to solve the exact problem you just ran into. Here is exactly what it does under the hood:

1. It Seals the "Sponge"

Raw pine is incredibly porous. If you throw regular paint directly onto it, the wood fibers instantly suck up the liquid, causing the paint to disappear and leaving a faint, uneven streak. Primer penetrates those pores and dries into a tough, impermeable plastic barrier, completely sealing the wood so your next layer of paint stays on the surface where it belongs.

2. It Gives the Paint "Teeth" to Grip

Regular paint doesn't stick well to slick or uneven surfaces. Primer dries to a slightly matte, microscopic rough texture (often called "teeth"). This gives the final coat of paint something physical to chemically bond and bite into, preventing it from peeling, cracking, or flaking off when the Iowa weather fluctuates between humid summers and freezing winters.

3. It Blocks Blemishes and Knots

Pine wood contains natural oils, sap, and dark knots. If you don't use a primer, those oils will eventually bleed right through regular white paint, turning your beautiful white hive yellow or brown in ugly spots. Primer acts as a shield that locks those oils deep inside the wood.

The Two Types You'll See at the Store

When you look at the shelves at Menards or Theisen's, you'll see two main choices:

  • Oil-Based / Alkyd Primer (Highly Recommended for Hives): This is the gold standard for raw wood. It blocks wood sap completely and doesn't raise the wood grain. It takes a bit longer to dry and requires mineral spirits to clean up, but it creates an absolute tank of a barrier.
  • Water-Based / Latex Primer: Easy cleanup with soap and water and dries incredibly fast (usually 30 minutes). While convenient, it doesn't block wood sap quite as well as oil-based options.

What to Grab

Look for a small quart of Exterior Wood Primer (brands like KILZ 2, KILZ Original, or Zinsser Bulls Eye 1-2-3 are classics).

Slap one coat of that onto the raw exterior of your hive box, wait for it to dry to the touch, and then hit it with your white paint. You will immediately notice a massive difference—the white paint will sit thick, bright, and solid on the very first pass.

turns.prompt_text: Sometimes I 3D print things with my red PLA, but I would like to paint them another color. Would just primer help do this, or do they need a different kind of thing?
turns.response_html:
Yes, primer is exactly what you need to paint your 3D prints!

Just like raw wood, 3D-printed plastic (like your Red PLA) has a unique surface texture that regular paint hates. If you try to paint directly onto raw PLA, the paint will bead up, pool in the layer lines, or easily scratch off with a fingernail.

Primer acts as the ultimate "chemical bridge" between the slick plastic and your new color coat.

Why Primer is a Game-Changer for 3D Prints

  • It Fills the Layer Lines: 3D prints have microscopic ridges from the printing process. Standard paint highlights these ridges. A good primer settles into those grooves, smoothing out the surface.
  • It Prevents the Red from "Bleeding": Red is a notoriously aggressive color. If you try to paint white or yellow directly over red plastic, the red will bleed through, making your final color look pink or muddy. Primer creates an opaque block.
  • It Gives the Paint "Teeth": PLA is very slick. Primer chemically bonds to the plastic and leaves a matte, slightly rough texture that gives your final spray paint or acrylics something to physically grip onto.

The Secret Weapon: "Filler Primer"

Instead of standard wood or wall primer, look for a can of Aerosol Spray Filler Primer (Rust-Oleum and Dupli-Color make great ones found in the automotive aisle at Menards, Theisen's, or any auto parts store in Ames).

[Raw PLA Layer Lines]  --->  [Filler Primer Fills Grooves]  --->  [Sanded Smooth]  --->  [Perfect Top Coat]
   /\/\/\/\/\/\/\                -----------------------          _______________        _______________

Filler primer is uniquely formulated to be much thicker than normal primer. It is designed to physically fill in minor imperfections, scratches, and—most importantly—your 3D print layer lines.

The 3D Print Painting Workflow

If you want to transform a red print into a flawless new color, use this quick protocol:

  1. Light Sanding (Optional but Recommended): Give the raw red print a quick rubdown with 220-grit sandpaper just to knock down any plastic burrs or sharp edges.
  2. Spray the Filler Primer: Shake the can vigorously and apply 2 to 3 thin, even coats of filler primer, waiting about 10 minutes between coats. Your print will look a boring, matte gray or brick red—this is exactly what you want.
  3. The Sanding Magic: Once dry (usually an hour), hit it lightly with 400-grit sandpaper. You will see the primer stay in the low grooves while exposing the high spots of the plastic, creating a perfectly smooth, flat surface.
  4. Paint Your New Color: Now, you can use whatever paint you want! Spray paint (like Rust-Oleum 2X) or hobby acrylics will stick beautifully and look incredibly professional.

Since you've got your Bambu Lab A1 dialled in for printing, adding a can of automotive filler primer to your workshop toolkit will completely change the quality of your finished visual projects.

However, there is one key mechanical difference to keep in mind so your topcoat behaves correctly: it won't be a clear coat, and it won't actually feel sticky or tacky to the touch.

Here is exactly how that layer works under the hood:

1. It’s Completely Opaque (Not Clear)

Unlike a clear topcoat that seals a finished piece, primer is highly pigmented and dries to a solid, flat color—usually matte gray, white, or dark brick red.

  • Why it's solid: This solid block of color behaves like a blank canvas. It completely blanks out the original aggressive color of your plastic or the dark knots in your wood so your final paint color shows up true and vibrant without getting muddied from underneath.

2. It Dries Smooth and Matte (Not Sticky)

When primer cures, it doesn't leave a sticky, glue-like residue. Instead, it dries completely dry to the touch, but with a microscopically rough, chalky texture.

  • The "Micro-Velcro" Effect: In the paint world, this texture is called "tooth." Think of it like microscopic Velcro. It gives the liquid molecules of your final paint layer something physical to bite into and lock onto. Without that matte texture, paint would just slide right off a slick 3D print or bead up unevenly.

How to Apply It

Because it acts as a separate structural layer, your application workflow looks like a sandwich:

[ Your Red PLA / Pine Wood ]

│  COLOR PAINT LAYER (1-2 Coats)         │ ──► Grips the primer; gives you the color
└────────────────────────────────────────┘

Quick Tips for Sprays vs. Brushes

  • For your 3D Prints: Spray-on primer (like an automotive filler primer) is highly recommended. Sprays apply an incredibly even, micro-thin mist that won't puddle or drown out the intricate hexagonal details of your designs.
  • For your Wooden Hive Boxes: A thick, brush-on exterior primer is perfect because you can aggressively work it into the thirsty pores of the pine to seal the wood.

turns.prompt_text: What's the difference between using primer alone and then paint after the primer has dried or just using paint and primer all in one?
turns.response_html:
This is one of the most common dilemmas in both DIY woodworking and 3D printing. The choice comes down to whether you are looking for maximum performance or convenience.

"Paint and Primer All-in-One" is a bit of a marketing misnomer. It doesn't actually contain a separate layer of primer floating inside the can. Instead, it is just a highly concentrated, extra-thick paint with higher solids and stronger binders than standard paint.

Here is how they stack up mechanically and when you should use each approach:

1. The Traditional Route: Separate Primer + Paint

This is the two-step process where you apply a dedicated primer layer, let it fully dry, and then apply your color topcoat.

  • How it works: The primer focuses 100% of its chemical formulation on bonding and sealing, while the paint focuses 100% of its formulation on color, durability, and finish (sheen).
  • The Advantage: It offers the absolute highest level of adhesion and protection. Because the primer is a separate chemical layer, it blocks stains, wood sap, and aggressive base colors (like your Red PLA) flawlessly.
  • The Effort: It takes longer because you have to wait for the primer to dry entirely before you can start painting your actual color.

2. The Modern Route: "Paint & Primer in One"

This is a single-product solution designed to skip a step in the workflow.

  • How it works: Because the paint is formulated to be much thicker and stickier than normal, it attempts to seal the surface and provide a vibrant color coat at the exact same time.
  • The Advantage: Speed. It saves you a massive amount of project time because you don't have to wait for a separate primer coat to cure. It works beautifully on surfaces that are already in good shape, previously painted, or slightly porous.
  • The Disadvantage: It doesn't have the same specialized capabilities as a standalone primer. It can struggle to block heavy stains, it won't fill 3D print layer lines smoothly, and aggressive plastics might still require multiple coats anyway to stop the original color from bleeding through.

Which One Should You Use?

To save yourself headache and extra trips to the hardware store, match the product to the material you are working on:

MaterialBest ChoiceWhy?
Raw Pine Wood (Like your Hive Box)Separate Primer + PaintRaw pine is incredibly "thirsty" and full of natural oils and knots. An all-in-one product will often sink right into the wood grain or let the knots bleed through over time. A dedicated exterior wood primer seals the "sponge" perfectly.
3D Prints (Like your Red PLA)Separate Primer + PaintSlick plastics need a dedicated chemical bond to prevent the paint from scratching off easily. Furthermore, using a specialized Aerosol Filler Primer allows you to fill in those tiny hexagonal layer lines for a completely smooth finish that all-in-one paint just can't achieve.
Pre-Painted Wood or Flat DrywallPaint & Primer in OneIf the surface is already sealed and you just want to change the color, an all-in-one is the perfect, time-saving tool for the job.

turns.prompt_text: What about epoxy?
turns.response_html:
Epoxy is like the "heavy artillery" of the coating world. While primer handles the chemical bond and paint handles the color, epoxy is an entirely different beast: it is a two-part liquid plastic (a resin and a hardener) that you mix together to trigger a chemical reaction, curing into a rock-hard, glassy, and completely waterproof armor shell.

For a wood-and-plastic hybrid build like your beekeeping frame components or custom visual 3D prints, epoxy can be a fantastic tool, but it serves a very different purpose than paint or primer.

Epoxy vs. Paint & Primer: The Core Differences

  • Thickness: Paint and primer go on in micro-thin layers measured in mils. Epoxy goes on thick, creating a heavy, structural layer that can bridge gaps, fix cracks, and completely encase a part.
  • Curing Mechanism: Paint and primer dry when their liquids evaporate into the air. Epoxy doesn't "dry"—it cures via an exothermic chemical reaction. This means it will cure perfectly even in thick layers or completely sealed spaces.
  • Surface Finish: It fills 3D print layer lines or rough wood grain entirely in a single coat, leaving a mirror-smooth, high-gloss finish.

How Epoxy Fits Into Your Toolkit

Because it cures into a solid, clear plastic shell, it has two massive use cases for the types of projects you build:

1. For Your 3D Prints: The Ultimate Layer-Line Eraser

If you want to smooth out a 3D print without spending hours sanding, a specialized thin epoxy coating (like XTC-3D) is a cheat code.

  • You brush a thin layer over your raw Red PLA, and it self-levels, filling all the microscopic hexagonal ridges and grooves perfectly.
  • Once it cures, your print looks like a smooth, injection-molded piece of plastic that you can then prime and paint flawlessly.

2. For Your Wood Projects: Structural Waterproofing

If you are joining 3D-printed PETG side bars to pine wood cross-beams, epoxy acts as an incredible gap-filling adhesive.

  • Unlike standard wood glue (like Titebond III), which needs tight wood-to-wood contact to work, epoxy can fill any loose "wobble" room inside a 3D-printed pocket or bracket, gluing the plastic to the wood with massive structural strength.

The Big Catch: UV Light

If you are thinking about using epoxy on the outside of your wooden beehive box to waterproof it, there is a major architectural catch: Standard epoxy hates the sun.

The intense UV rays from the Iowa sun will cause standard epoxy to turn yellow, become brittle, and crack within a single season. If you want to use it outdoors, you have to buy a specific UV-resistant Marine Grade Epoxy (the kind used on boats), or you have to paint over the cured epoxy with a solid exterior paint to shield it from the sun.

Summary: When to Use What

If your goal is to...Use...
Change the color and protect raw wood/plastic from the elementsPrimer + Exterior Paint
Completely hide 3D print layer lines for a smooth, glassy finishEpoxy Coating (or Filler Primer for a matte finish)
Permanently bond 3D-printed plastic components to woodTwo-Part Epoxy Glue

turns.response_html:
You hit on the two most important points when considering epoxy: it is definitely a premium product that impacts your wallet, and because it involves a chemical reaction, it requires some basic safety respect.

Here is the honest breakdown on the cost and safety of using epoxy for your projects.

1. Is Epoxy Expensive? (The Cost Reality)

Yes, compared to a $10 can of spray paint or a $15 quart of primer, epoxy is significantly more expensive.

  • The Price Tag: A basic starter kit of standard two-part total boat or art epoxy (around 16 to 32 ounces total) typically runs between $25 and $45. If you scale up to a full gallon kit for large woodworking projects, you are looking at $80 to $150+.
  • Why it costs more: You aren't buying liquid pigment that evaporates; you are buying high-density liquid polymers. 100% of what you pour out of the bottles stays on the project as solid plastic.
  • Is it worth it? For structural bonding (like securing your 3D-printed PETG side bars to pine wood) or for sealing a custom visual print to a mirror finish, a little goes a long way. You only need a thin brush coat, so a $30 kit will last you through several projects.

2. Is Epoxy Safe?

The short answer is yes, once it is fully cured (hardened), it is completely safe and inert. In fact, cured epoxy is incredibly stable and completely non-toxic.

However, while it is a liquid and actively curing, it is a chemical process that you need to handle with care. Here are the safety rules to follow in your workshop:

  • Skin Contact (The Biggest Risk): Liquid epoxy resin and hardener can cause severe skin irritation or chemical burns. Over time, repeated skin exposure can cause you to develop a permanent allergy to it. Always wear nitrile gloves when mixing and pouring. If you get it on your hands, don't use solvents to clean it—use soap, warm water, or a dedicated citrus-based hand cleaner.
  • Fumes and Ventilation: While some modern epoxies are labeled "Low Odor" or "VOC-Free," the chemical reaction still releases microscopic vapors. Always mix and apply epoxy in a well-ventilated space (like a garage with the door cracked, or near an open window with a fan blowing outward). If you are sanding cured epoxy down later, wear a standard dust mask so you don't inhale the fine plastic airborne dust.
  • The "Exothermic" Heat: Epoxy creates heat as it cures. If you mix a large batch in a plastic cup and just leave it sitting there, it can get hot enough to melt the cup, smoke, or burn your hand. Only mix what you need, and pour it out onto your flat project surface quickly so the heat can dissipate safely.

The Beekeeping Exception: Is it Safe for Bees?

If you are thinking about using epoxy anywhere near your hive components:

  • Glued Joints: Using it as an adhesive inside the enclosed joints of your hybrid frames is 100% safe once it has cured for 24–48 hours and has zero chemical smell left.
  • Coating Frames: I would avoid coating the actual face of your 3D-printed foundations with epoxy. Bees are incredibly sensitive to chemical scents, and they prefer the raw, textured surface of your PLA mesh anyway—especially once you hit it with that thin layer of melted beeswax.

turns.prompt_text: How did we discover this stuff?
turns.response_html:
The story of how we discovered epoxy is a classic tale of industrial chemistry chemistry, where two different scientists working on opposite sides of the Atlantic Ocean accidentally stumbled onto the exact same chemical breakthrough at nearly the exact same time.

Before the 1930s, the world didn't have super-strong, gap-filling synthetic plastics that could bond anything to anything. We relied on natural glues (like boiled animal hides) or early plastics like Bakelite, which were brittle.

Here is the timeline of how two inventors cracked the code:

1. The German Breakthrough (1934)

The first person to successfully synthesize epoxy resin was a German chemist named Paul Schlack.

  • He wasn't actually trying to invent the world's strongest glue; he was working for a massive chemical conglomerate trying to find a way to create new synthetic textiles and fibers (competing with Nylon).
  • Schlack mixed an organic compound called bisphenol-A (BPA) with a highly reactive chemical called epichlorohydrin.
  • He noticed that when these reacted, they formed a liquid polymer that polymerizes into a tough, resilient plastic when mixed with a hardening agent. He locked down a German patent for it in 1934.

2. The Swiss Dentist Connection (1936)

Meanwhile, a Swiss chemist named Dr. Pierre Castan was approaching the problem from a completely different angle. He was trying to find a synthetic material to make better dental crowns and artificial teeth.

  • He needed a liquid material that could be poured into a mold of a mouth, wouldn't shrink as it hardened, and would be completely inert and safe once cured.
  • Working independently, Castan mixed the exact same chemical combination (BPA and epichlorohydrin).
  • He realized that the resulting resin could be mixed with a liquid hardener (a "cross-linking agent") to form a rock-hard, glossy substance. While it didn't end up revolutionizing dentistry, Castan immediately recognized its incredible properties as an adhesive and casting resin. He filed for patents in 1936.

Commercializing the Liquid Armor

Because Castan's Swiss company didn't have the massive manufacturing power to produce this stuff at scale, they licensed his patents to a Swiss chemical company called CIBA (which later became part of Novartis and Huntsman).

CIBA brought it to the public market at the 1946 Swiss Industries Fair under the brand name Araldite, marketing it as a miracle structural adhesive.

At the exact same time in the United States, a company called DeVoe & Raynolds was working on the same chemistry to invent better coatings and varnishes for ships and industrial machinery. They developed their own processes and eventually laid the groundwork for the modern epoxy marine resins we use today.

Why It Was Such a Big Deal

Before epoxy, "drying" meant waiting for water or alcohol to evaporate out of paint or glue, which always caused the material to shrink, crack, or warp.

The discovery of epoxy introduced thermosetting polymers to the DIY and industrial world—meaning you could mix two stable liquids together, throw them in a vacuum, underwater, or inside a sealed wooden joint, and they would perfectly transform into a completely solid piece of custom plastic through their own internal chemical heat.

It is pretty incredible that the same chemical reaction you can use to bridge a gap between your 3D-printed PETG side bars and your pine wood top bars today was originally invented to create synthetic clothing and fake teeth!
